# whose-code-site

> Public case study for whose-code: we scanned 34,012 commits of our own agent-built code with our authorship scanner and published the complete result, warts and all — including a disclosed correction after we found and fixed the scanner's own blind spot.

whose-code-site is maintained by Adventure Wave Labs (The lab for agentic developer tooling).

## The receipt (method v0.2, re-cut 2026-11-19)

| repo | commits | assisted | machine | unknown | velocity flags | merges w/ review evidence | gate runs | classed w/o confession |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| turbo-rig | 31,967 | 13 | 0 | 31,954 | 0 | 132 / 132 | 743 | 0 |
| ancuria | 1,893 | 614 | 0 | 1,279 | 152 | 102 / 102 | 692 | 0 |
| adventure-wave-explorer | 152 | 0 | 4 | 148 | 0 | 11 / 11 | 64 | 0 |

Correction, disclosed: the Nov 7 receipt showed 0 assisted on turbo-rig and 37 on ancuria. The scanner's identity rules could not match real agent trailers (model-suffixed names like "Claude Opus 5.5", lab identities like "zcode"). Found by dogfooding, fixed through the same public review gate, receipt re-cut.

## The zero, stated precisely

No commit was classified assisted or machine at deciding confidence without a
direct confession — on these repos, under this method. That is what the zero
can prove: indirect signals never decided a class. It is not a general
accuracy guarantee. Classes are assisted / machine / unknown; there is no
"human" class by design — commit messages can prove machine involvement, never
human authorship.
